The meaning of the statement seems to be: no sinner bears the sin of another, but each soul has its own sin, not the sin of other souls.

As follows:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾: By Allah, Allah does not place upon a servant the sin of another, and He does not hold anyone accountable except for his own deed.

* *

As for His words ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾

Allah, may He be remembered, says: We would not destroy any people except after giving them warning through messengers and establishing the proof against them through signs that cut off their excuse.

As follows:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾: Indeed, Allah, blessed and exalted, does not punish anyone until a report from Allah reaches him beforehand, or a clear proof comes to him from Allah, and He punishes no one except for his sin.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: On the Day of Resurrection, Allah, blessed and exalted, will gather the souls of those who died in the interval (fatrah), the insane, the deaf, the mute, and the senile elders to whom Islam came when they had grown senile. Then He will send a messenger to them, [saying]: "Enter the Fire." They will say: "How, when no messenger came to us? By Allah, if they entered it, it would be coolness and safety for them." Then He will send to them, and whoever would have obeyed Him before will obey Him. Abu Hurayrah said: Recite if you wish: ﴿And We would never punish until We sent a messenger﴾.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Hammam, from Abu Hurayrah, similarly.

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 16:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein; so the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction﴾ (17:16).

The reciters differed over the recitation of His words ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾. The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Iraq recited ﴿amarna﴾ with a short alif (qasr), without elongation, and with a light (takhfif) mim, vowelled with a fatha. When it is recited thus, the most prevalent interpretation is: We commanded its affluent ones with obedience, and they transgressed therein through their disobedience to God and their opposition to His command. Many of those who recited it thus also interpreted it this way.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn Abbas said regarding ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾: "With obedience to God, but they disobeyed."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Sharik narrated to us, from Salama or another, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "We commanded them with obedience, but they disobeyed." It may also be possible, if it is recited thus, that its meaning is: "We made them leaders, and they transgressed therein," because the Arabs say: "He is a commander who is not commanded." Some of the scholars of Arabic speech from the people of Basra used to say: its meaning, when recited thus, may be directed toward the sense of "We multiplied its affluent ones," and he supports this interpretation by the report transmitted from the Messenger of God ﷺ, that he said: "The best property is a mare that is ma'mura, or a palm-grove that is ma'bura." He says that the meaning of "ma'mura" is "abundant in offspring." Some of the scholars of Arabic speech from the Kufans rejected this from him, and did not permit "amarna" in the sense of "akthharna" except with an elongated alif in "amarna." He says regarding "mahra ma'mura": it was only said thus by way of conformity (ittiba') because "ma'bura" comes after it, just as it was said: "Return, you women, ma'zurat, not ma'jurat," so the hamza of "ma'zurat" follows the hamza of "ma'jurat," and it derives from "wazara," by way of conforming one part of speech to another. Abu Uthman recited it as ﴿ammarna﴾ with a doubled mim, in the sense of rule (imara).

Hadith: Hanad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Ikrima, regarding His words ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾: "We multiplied them." (Note: this line appears in the source under the isnad of Ahmad ibn Yusuf narrating from al-Qasim from Hushaym from Awf from Abu Uthman al-Nahdi that he recited ﴿ammarna﴾ with shadda from imara.) Several people of interpretation also interpreted this passage in this sense.

Mention of those who said this:

Ali ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿ammarna mutrafiha﴾, he says: "We empowered its wicked ones, and they disobeyed therein; when they did that, I destroyed them with punishment," which is His words: ﴿And thus We placed in every town its greatest criminals to plot therein﴾ (6:123).

Al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Kisai narrate from Abu Ja'far al-Razi, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, that he recited it ﴿ammarna﴾ and said: "We empowered."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Hafs, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliya, who said: ﴿ammarna﴾ with the heavy form: "We made over it its affluent ones, its arrogant ones."

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, both from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿ammarna mutrafiha﴾, he said: "We sent."

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

It is reported from al-Hasan al-Basri that he recited it ﴿aamarna﴾ with an elongated alif in "amarna," in the sense of "we multiplied its wicked ones." Several people of interpretation also directed the meaning of this word to this interpretation, except that those who transmitted to us did not distinguish for us the differences of recitation in this, and how those who interpreted it recited it, except a few of them.

Mention of one who interpreted it thus: Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones—aamarna mutrafiha—and they transgress therein﴾, he says: "We multiplied their number."

Hanad narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Simak, from Ikrima, regarding His words ﴿aamarna mutrafiha﴾, he said: "We multiplied them."

Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayya narrated to us, from Abu Raja', from al-Hasan, regarding His words ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾, he said: "We multiplied them."

I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Abd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾: "We multiplied its affluent ones," that is, its nobles.

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones—aamarna mutrafiha—and they transgress therein, so the word becomes due against it﴾, he says: "We multiplied its affluent ones, that is, its tyrants; they transgressed therein and acted in disobedience to God," ﴿so We destroyed it with complete destruction﴾. It was said: when God intends good for a people, He sends them a reformer; when He intends corruption for them, He sends them a corrupter; and when He intends to destroy a town, He multiplies its affluent ones.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿aamarna mutrafiha﴾, he said: "We multiplied them."

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ entered upon Zaynab one day while saying: "There is no god but God. Woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near. Today there has been opened from the barrier of Gog and Magog such as this," and he made a circle between his thumb and the finger next to it. She said: "O Messenger of God, will we be destroyed while the righteous are among us?" He said: "Yes, when wickedness increases."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they defiantly transgress therein﴾: "Some people of knowledge mentioned that amarna means: we multiplied." He said: The Arabs say of a large thing "amira" because of its abundance. As for when a people is described as having increased, it is said: "The sons of so-and-so became numerous (amara)," and "the people become numerous (ya'muru) and their affair grew great," as Labid said:

"If they are envied, they will be destroyed; and if they become numerous (amiru) one day, they will come to scarcity and ruin."

[[The verse is in the Diwan of Labid, printed in Leiden in 1880, the version of al-Tusi, p. 19. In his version the last line reads "lil-halak wal-nakad" in place of "lil-qall wal-naqad." In the author's version, its commentator said: "He says: if they are envied one day, they will die; yahbitu here means they will die. Abu al-Hasan said: this is the view of Abu Amr. It is also transmitted: 'yughbatu': they die of envy, as if they die without illness. A camel slaughtered without cause is called i'tabata, taken from al-'abit, and al-'abit is the fresh of everything." End quote. I say: al-qadd and al-naqd mean scarcity and wealth.]]

The verbal noun is "al-amr," and the noun is "al-imr," as God, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿You have certainly brought a thing terrible (imran)﴾ (18:74). It is also said in the proverb "an evil imr," meaning abundant.

The most correct of the recitations in my view is the recitation of those who recited ﴿amarna mutrafiha﴾ with a short alif in "amarna" and a light mim, because the authoritative reciters have agreed upon its correctness to the exclusion of others. Since this is the more correct recitation, the most fitting interpretation of it is the interpretation of those who understood: "We commanded its people with obedience, and they transgressed therein and disobeyed, so the word became due against them," because the most prevalent meaning of "amarna" is "command," which is the opposite of prohibition and no other, and directing the meanings of the speech of God, exalted is His praise, toward its most well-known and recognised meanings is more fitting than any other way of proceeding.

The meaning of His words ﴿fa-fasaqu fiha﴾ is: they opposed the command of God therein and departed from His obedience. ﴿fa-haqqa 'alayha al-qawl﴾ means: it became binding upon them, through their disobedience to God and their transgression therein, the threat of God which He had promised to whoever disbelieved in Him and opposed His messengers, of destruction after admonition and warning through the messengers and proofs. ﴿fa-dammarnaha tadmira﴾ means: We then ruined it with complete ruin, and destroyed those of its people who were in it with destruction, as al-Farazdaq said:

"They were to them like the young camel of Thamud, when it bellowed, the back-bending, and he destroyed them with destruction."

[[The verse is by al-Farazdaq (Diwan, p. 443), cited by the author as evidence that His words "fadammarnaha tadmira" mean: "we ruined it with ruin."]]

The verse is from a poem in which al-Farazdaq contested the qasida of Jarir, whose opening line is:

"Greetings to the abodes of Su'ad, indeed I love, for love of Fatima, al-Dhiyar."

The pronoun in his words "and they were to them like the young camel of Thamud" refers to Jarir mentioned in the preceding verse, which is:

"Dragging the disgraceful ones upon Kulayb, Jarir, then he did not prevent the destruction (al-dammar)."

Bakr Thamud: the young camel of the prophet Salih. Raghaa: a sound. Al-ragha'": the sound of animals with hoofs.

Commentary on the verse: "How many generations have We destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord, as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants." (17:17)

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And how many generations We destroyed after Noah. And sufficient is your Lord, as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants﴾

This is a warning from God, the Exalted and Remembered, to the deniers of His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) among the polytheists of Quraysh, a threat of punishment against them, and an announcement from Him to them that if they do not desist from what they persist in, namely their denial of His Messenger (ﷺ), then His wrath will descend upon them and there will come down upon them of His punishment what came down upon the nations before them who followed the path of disbelief in God and denial of His messengers. God, the Exalted and Remembered, says: "Indeed We have destroyed, O people, before you, after Noah, down to your time, many generations who were in rejection of God's signs and disbelief in Him and denial of His messengers, in the same manner as you are. And you are not more honored before God, the Exalted, than they were, for there is no kinship between anyone and God, may His praise be great, such that He would punish one people for what He does not punish others, or pardon the sins of some people and then punish others for them." He, may His praise be great, says: "So turn back in obedience to God your Lord, for We have sent to you a messenger who will remind you of Our proofs against you and awaken you from your heedlessness, and We would not punish a people until We send to them a messenger warning them of the proofs of God, while you persist in your transgression." And "sufficient is your Lord, O Muhammad, as Knower of the sins of His servants": that is, "sufficient for you is God, O Muhammad, as one who is informed and knowing of the sins of His creation, for nothing of the deeds of these polytheists of your people is hidden from Him, nor the deeds of others among His creation. He knows all of that and is Informed and Seeing." He says: "He sees all of that, and nothing of it is absent from Him, nor is an atom's weight on earth or in heaven hidden from Him, nor anything smaller than that or greater."

It has been disputed regarding the duration of a qarn (generation/century):

Mujahid ibn Musa narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Hammad ibn Salamah narrated to us, from Abu Muhammad, Abd Allah ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "The qarn is one hundred and twenty years. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent in the first qarn that existed, and the last of them was Yazid ibn Mu'awiya."

Others said: Rather, it is one hundred years.

Mention of those who said that:

❖ Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Himsi Abu al-Sult al-Ta'i narrated to us, he said: Salamah ibn Hawwas narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, from Abd Allah ibn Busr al-Mazini, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) placed his hand on his head and said: "This boy will live a qarn." I said: "How long is a qarn?" He said: "One hundred years."

❖ Hasan ibn Muhammad narrated to us, he said: Salamah ibn Hawwas narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, who said: "We kept counting for him until one hundred years were completed, and then he died." Abu al-Sult said: Salamah informed me that this Muhammad ibn al-Qasim was the son-in-law (khatn) of Abd Allah ibn Busr.

Others said concerning this:

❖ Isma'il ibn Musa al-Fazari narrated to us, he said: Umar ibn Shakir informed us, from Ibn Sirin, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The qarn is forty years."

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord﴾

The letter bā' (ب) was introduced in His saying ﴿bi-Rabbika (by your Lord)﴾, although it is in a position of nominative case (raf'), because the meaning of the sentence is: "Sufficient for you is your Lord, and adequate is your Lord, as Knower of the sins of His servants," indicating praise. The Arabs do this in every sentence that carries the meaning of praise or blame: they introduce the bā' into a noun, and the noun into which the bā' is introduced is in the nominative position, so that its introduction indicates praise or blame, as in their sayings: "How honorable a man he is (akrim bihi rajulan)," "Your companion is sufficient as a man (nahīka bihi rajulan)," "Your garment is generous as a garment (jada bi-thawbika thawban)," "Your food is good as food (tāba bi-ta'āmikum ta'āman)," and what resembles such speech. Were the bā' removed from these nouns into which it was introduced, they would be in the nominative, because they are in the nominative position, as the poet said:

"He tells me of the absent man through his conduct; / Conduct suffices, though it does not inform of what the man has concealed."

Note: This verse is cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (Jami'a microfilm no. 24059, p. 178), who said: "Every instance in the Qur'an of His saying 'sufficient is your Lord,' and 'sufficient is God,' and 'sufficient against yourself today': if the bā' were dropped, the noun would be nominative, as the poet said: 'He tells me ... (the verse)'. The introduction of the bā' into a nominative is permitted only when it is used to praise its owner. Do you not see that you say: 'Sufficient is he for you (kafāka bihi),' 'Forbidden is he (nahāka bihi),' 'How honorable a man (akrim bihi rajulan),' 'How wretched a man (bi'sa bihi rajulan),' 'How excellent a man (ni'ma bihi rajulan),' 'Good is your food as food (tāba bi-ta'āmika ta'āman),' 'Generous is your garment as a garment (jāda bi-thawbika thawban)'? If it were not praise or blame, the introduction would not be permitted. Do you not see that one who says 'your brother came' or 'your brother sat' may not say 'came with your brother' or 'sat with your brother' unless he means 'another came with him' or 'another sat with him'?" End of quotation. The author has taken from al-Farra's words as he pleased, though he did not attribute it to its speaker in this place.

However, when there is no praise or blame in the sentence, they do not introduce the bā' into the noun; it is not permissible to say "came with your brother" when you mean "your brother came," unless you mean "another man came with him," and that is a meaning different from the first.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 18:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the fleeting [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have appointed for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished.﴾ (17:18)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Whoever's aim is the fleeting worldly life, for which alone he works and strives, and which alone he seeks, not believing in a return (to God), and not hoping for reward or punishment from his Lord for his deeds: ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend﴾. That is: God hastens for him in this world whatever He wills of spreading out worldly provision upon him, or restricting it for whomever God intends to do that to, or destroying him with whatever punishments He wills. ﴿Then We have appointed for him Hell, which he will enter﴾: that is, then We cause him to burn in Hell when he comes to Us in the Hereafter, ﴿blamed﴾ for his scant gratitude toward Us and his evil conduct regarding the favors he received from Us in the world, ﴿banished﴾: that is, removed and driven away, cast out into the Fire.

And in accordance with what we have said regarding this, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said:

Mention of those who said this:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿Whoever desires the fleeting [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend﴾: that is, whoever has the world as his concern, his preoccupation, his seeking, and his intention, God hastens for him therein what He wills, then compels him toward Hell. He said: ﴿Then We have appointed for him Hell, which he will enter, blamed and banished﴾: blamed in the bounty of God, banished from the punishment of God.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Tayyibah, a shaykh from the people of al-Massisah, told me that he heard Abu Ishaq al-Fazari say regarding ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend﴾: "for whom We intend" means for whom We intend destruction.

Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: Abdullah narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿blamed﴾: it means reproached.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿Whoever desires the fleeting [life], We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We intend﴾: "the fleeting" means the world.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 19:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it, while being a believer—those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Whoever desires the Hereafter and seeks it, and performs for it the deed that is its due, which is obedience to God and what pleases Him. He attributed the striving to the pronoun (the hāʾ and alif), which refers to the Hereafter, so that it means: he strove for the Hereafter with the striving of the Hereafter. The meaning is: and worked for it the work due to it, so that the listeners understand the sense of it. The meaning is that he strove for it with the striving due to it, while being a believer. He says: he is a believer who affirms God's reward and the greatness of His recompense for his striving for it, not denying it in the manner of one who desires the immediate life. God, exalted is His praise, says ﴿Then those﴾, meaning: whoever does that, ﴿their striving was﴾, meaning their deeds in obedience to God, ﴿appreciated﴾. God's appreciation of their striving is the goodness of His recompense to them for their righteous deeds, and His overlooking of their evil deeds through His mercy.

As related:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it, while being a believer—those are the ones whose striving will be appreciated﴾: God's appreciation of their good deeds, and His overlooking of their evil deeds.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 20:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To each — these and those — We extend from the bounty of your Lord. And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted, means: Your Lord, O Muhammad, extends to both groups — those who desire the hastened (al-'ajilah, this worldly life) and those who desire the Hereafter, those who strive for it while being believers — from His bounty in this world, so He provides for both of them from His provision until they reach their appointed term and fulfil the lifespan decreed for them. Then their states diverge after death, and they separate after arriving at the place of return: the group that desired the hastened life has Hell as their destination of return, and the group that desired the Hereafter has Paradise as their final abode. ﴿And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted﴾ means: the bounty of your Lord, which He gives to whomever He wills of His creatures in this world, is not withheld from the one to whom He extends it, and none of His creatures can prevent Him from that, and God has indeed given it to him.

Those who interpret the Qur'an (ahl al-ta'wil) have said similarly to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said that:

Qatadah, regarding His saying (﴿To each — these and those — We extend from the bounty of your Lord. And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted﴾): i.e., diminished. Indeed, God, mighty and majestic, has apportioned the world between the righteous and the wicked, while the Hereafter is exclusively for the God-fearing with your Lord.

Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, ﴿And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted﴾, he said: diminished.

Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Makhrami narrated to us, he said: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi narrated to us, he said: Sahl ibn Abi al-Salt al-Sarraj narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Hasan say, ﴿To each — these and those — We extend from the bounty of your Lord﴾, he said: We give from the world to the righteous and the wicked alike.

al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn 'Abbas said, ﴿Whoever desires the hastened, We hasten for him therein what We will﴾ ... the verse ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter﴾ ... then He said ﴿To each — these and those — We extend from the bounty of your Lord﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: He provides for the one who desires the world, and He provides for the one who desires the Hereafter. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted﴾, he said: withheld.

Bishr narrated to us, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿To each — these and those﴾: the people of the world and the people of the Hereafter, ﴿from the bounty of your Lord. And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted﴾, he said: withheld.

Yunus narrated to me, he said: Ibn Wahb informed us, he said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His saying ﴿To each — these and those﴾: the people of the world and the people of the Hereafter, ﴿from the bounty of your Lord. And the bounty of your Lord is never restricted﴾, from the righteous or the wicked. He said: al-mahzur means the withheld. And he recited ﴿See how We have favored some of them over others; and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in preference.﴾

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 21:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Behold how We have favoured some of them over others. But the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favour﴾.

He, exalted be His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Look, O Muhammad, with the eye of your heart at these two groups: one of them desires the immediate abode and seeks it and works for it, and the other desires the Hereafter and strives for it, certain of God's reward for its striving. Behold how We favoured one of the two groups over the other, by giving this one insight into its right course, guiding it to the path that is most upright, and facilitating for it what is most guided and rightly directed, while We forsook this other one, leading it astray from the way of truth and blinding its sight to the path of right guidance. ﴿But the Hereafter is greater in degrees﴾: he says, the group that desires the Hereafter is greater in the Hereafter in degrees, some over others, due to the differences of their ranks by their deeds in Paradise, ﴿and greater in favour﴾, by God's favouring some of them over others, from those other groups in this world, in what We have extended to them in it.

Al-Tabari said: Similar to what we have said in this regard is what the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿Behold how We have favoured some of them over others﴾: i.e., in this world. ﴿But the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favour﴾: indeed the believers in Paradise have ranks, and they have virtues according to their deeds. It was related to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, between the highest people of Paradise and the lowest in rank is like the star that is seen in the eastern and western horizons."

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not set up another god alongside God, lest you sit down reproached and forsaken﴾.

He, dhikruhu (exalted is He), says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Do not, O Muhammad, set up a partner with God in His divinity and worship. Rather, devote worship sincerely to Him and single Him out for divinity, for there is no god but Him. For if you set up with Him another god, and worship someone other than Him alongside Him, you will sit down reproached: that is, you will become blameworthy for having neglected to thank God for the blessings He has bestowed upon you, and for having given thanks to someone other than the One who conferred the favour upon you, and for associating in praise someone who had no share with Him in the blessing bestowed upon you. Forsaken: your Lord will have abandoned you to whoever seeks evil against you. And if your Lord, who is the helper of His friends, abandons you, then you will have no protector besides Him who will support you and ward off harm from you.

As related:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿Do not set up another god alongside God, lest you sit down reproached and forsaken﴾, he said: "Reproached for the blessing of God."

This statement, although it was addressed in the form of an address to the Prophet of God (ﷺ), is meant for everyone among the servants of God, mighty and majestic, who bears the obligation of religious duty.

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a generous word.﴾ (17:23)

He, exalted is His remembrance, means by this: the judgment of your Lord, O Muhammad, by His command to you that you not worship anyone except Allah, for none should be worshipped other than Him. The wording of the people of ta'wil (interpretation, explanation of meaning) differed regarding His words ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾, although their meanings all amount to one thing.

Mention of what they said about this:

Ali ibn Dawud related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾: he says, "He commanded."

Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir related to us, saying: Zakariyya ibn Salam related to us, saying: A man came to al-Hasan and said: "He divorced his wife three times." He said: "You have disobeyed your Lord, and your wife is separated from you." The man said: "God decreed that upon me." Al-Hasan, who was eloquent, said: "What God decreed is what God commanded," and he recited this verse: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾. The people then said: "Al-Hasan has spoken about predestination (qadar)."

Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding His words ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾: meaning, your Lord commanded that you not worship anyone but Him. "This is God's immediate decree." It was said in some wisdom: "Whoever pleases his parents, has pleased his Creator; and whoever angers his parents, has angered his Lord."

Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, he said: "He commanded that you not worship anyone but Him." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: ﴿And your Lord has enjoined (wassa) that you worship none but Him﴾.

Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Isa related to us, saying: Nusayr ibn Abi al-Ash'ath related to us, saying: Ibn Habib ibn Abi Thabit related to me, from his father, who said: Ibn Abbas gave me a mushaf (copy of the Qur'an) and said: "This is according to the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b." Abu Kurayb said: Yahya said: "I saw the mushaf with Nusayr, in which was: ﴿And your Lord has enjoined (wa-wassa)﴾," meaning: "and decreed (wa-qada)."

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾, he said: "And your Lord has enjoined (awsa)."

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾: "He commanded that you not worship anyone but Him."

al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Qasim related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Abu Ishaq al-Kufi, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, that he recited it as ﴿And your Lord has enjoined (wa-wassa)﴾, and said: "They attached the waw to the sad so it became qaf."

* *

As for His words ﴿and that you be good to parents﴾:

He says: and He commanded you to be good to parents, that you act kindly toward them and show them dutifulness. The meaning of the speech is: "And He commanded you that you be good to the parents." Since "an" (that) was omitted, the decree was attached to the kindness, as one says in speech: "I command you to do good to him," and "I enjoin you to do good to him," meaning: "I command you that you do good to him." Then "an" is omitted, so that the command and the enjoining become attached to the good itself, as the poet said:

"I marvelled at Dahma'a when she complained to us,
and at Abu Dahma'a when he enjoined us
to good by them, as if we were ungenerous to them."

[The three verses are from the metre of rajaz. They are among the evidences cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (p. 178). He said: The Arabs say: "I enjoin you to it (awsika bihi) as good," and "I command you to it as good," and the meaning is: "I command you to do good to him." Then "an" is omitted, so the good is connected to the enjoining and the commanding. The poet said: "I marvelled ... (the verses)."]

And the verb yuwsina (enjoins us) acts upon the good.

The reciters differed regarding the recitation of His words ﴿Whether one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. The majority of reciters of Medina and Basra, and some reciters of Kufa, recited ﴿Whether he reaches (yablughanna)﴾ in the singular, directing it to one of them, since "one of them" is singular; so they made the verb singular to match, and made His words ﴿or both of them﴾ conjoined with "one of them." The majority of Kufan reciters recited ﴿Whether both of them reach (yablughana)﴾ in the dual, with the nun pronounced and doubled, and they said: "The two parents have already been mentioned, and His words ﴿reach (yablughan)﴾ are a predicate about them after their names were mentioned." They said: "When the verb comes after the noun, the speech should have evidence that it is a predicate about two or a group." They said: "The evidence that it is a predicate about two in the imperfect verb is the alif and nun." They said: "And His words ﴿one of them or both of them﴾ are a new sentence, as is said: ﴿They were blind and deaf; then God turned to them; then many of them became blind and deaf﴾, and as in His words ﴿and they conspired secretly﴾, then He began: ﴿those who did wrong﴾."

The more correct of the two recitations in my view is the one who recited ﴿Whether he reaches (yablughanna)﴾ in the singular, as a predicate about one of them, because the statement about kindness toward the parents had ended at His words ﴿and that you be good to parents﴾, and then He began: ﴿Whether one of them or both of them reach old age with you﴾.

* *

As for His words ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾:

He says: do not say "uff" (expression of annoyance) at anything you see from either of them, or from both, by which people are harmed; rather, bear patiently from them, and count your patience toward them as an act reckoned for reward, just as they were patient with you in your childhood.

The people of ta'wil said things similar to what we have said.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Muhabbab related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Layth, from Mujahid, regarding His words ﴿So do not say to them "uff" nor rebuke them﴾: he said: "If they reach old age with you to the point that they urinate and defecate, then do not say to them 'uff', out of disgust at them."

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "Whether they reach old age with you, so do not say to them 'uff' when you see the filth, and remove for them the excrement and urine, as they removed it for you when you were small, and do not hurt them."

The people of knowledge of the speech of the Arabs have differed regarding the meaning of "uff." Some of them said: its meaning is: whatever is coarse in speech and ugly.

Others said: "uff" is the dirt under the fingernails, and whatever you lift from the ground with your hand of something insignificant. The Arabs have six dialectal pronunciations of "uff": with and without tanwin (nunation), in the nominative, genitive, and accusative. Whoever read it in the genitive with tanwin, which is the recitation of the majority of the people of Medina, likened it to sounds that have no meaning, like their saying in imitating a sound "ghaq ghaq" (cawing). They put a kasra on the fa and made it nunated, though its original state is sukun (quiescence), since no grammatical factor makes it inflect, owing to its coming after a quiescent letter, the alif. They disliked bringing two quiescent letters together, so they moved it to the nearest vowel to sukun, which is kasra, since the jazm (apocopated) form when moved is moved to kasra.

As for those who read it in the genitive without tanwin, which is the recitation of the majority of the reciters of Kufa and Basra, they said: nunation is added only to sounds that come incomplete, like "mah," "sah," and "bakh," which are completed with tanwin because they fall short of the nominal patterns. They said: "uff" is complete and needs nothing else to complete it, since it has come in three letters. They said: "We pronounced the second fa with kasra so as not to bring together two quiescent letters."

As for whoever read it with a damma and tanwin, he said: it is a noun like other nouns that are known, and not a sound, and it was turned away from being a sound. And as for whoever read it with a damma without tanwin, he said: it is not an inflecting noun, so it does not take the inflection of declinable nouns; they said: we pronounce it with damma as we pronounce His words ﴿To God belongs the command, before and after﴾, and as we pronounce a noun in the single vocative, so we say: "O Zayd." Whoever read it with a fatha without tanwin, which is the recitation of some Meccans and the people of Syria, likened it to their saying "madd, ya hadha" and "radd." Whoever read it with a fatha and tanwin made the verb operate upon it, and made it a sound noun, so one says: "I did not say to him: 'uffan' nor 'tuffan'."

Some grammarians of Basra used to say: It has been recited as "uff," and "uffa" is a dialect in which they made it like its adjective. Some read "uffin," because some Arabs say "uffa laka" by way of quotation, meaning: "Do not say this statement to them." He said: the raising (damma) is ugly, because nothing comes after it with a lam. Those who said "uffin" with a kasra are many, and it is the better. Some used kasra with tanwin. Some said "uffi," as if he attributed this statement to himself, saying: "uffi for this for both of you." The kasra form of this word is nunated and non-nunated, as an indeclinable noun, like "amsa" and what resembles it, and the fatha form without tanwin is similarly indeclinable.

Some people of Arabic said: all six vowel patterns enter into "uff" as quotation, resembling a noun at one time and a sound at another. He said: Sounds are most often given kasra with tanwin when they are of two letters, like "sah," "mah," and "bakh." When they are of three letters they resemble particles, like "layta" and "madda," and "uffa" like "mudda" which resembles particles, and "uff" as "sahha." They said: "I heard 'mid' (Ya hadha) and 'midd,'" and it is related from al-Kisa'i that he said: "I heard: 'What taught you that, your family, except "mid" and "midd"'," and this is like "iff" and "uff." Whoever said "uffan" made it like "suhqan" and "bu'dan."

The more correct in my view regarding the reading of this word is the recitation of the one who recited ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾ with a kasra on the fa, without tanwin, for two reasons: first, it is the most famous and the most eloquent of the dialects of the Arabs in it; second, that the lot of everything that has no declinable form in speech is sukun. Since this is so, and the fa in "uff" is by right to be a pause, and there was no way to that because of the meeting of two quiescent letters in it, and the rule of a quiescent letter when it is moved is that it be moved to kasra, it was moved to kasra, as is said: "mudda," "shuddu," and "rudda al-bab" (close the door).

* *

As for His words ﴿nor rebuke them﴾:

He, exalted is His praise, says: nor drive them away harshly.

As:

Muhammad ibn Isma'il al-Ahmasi related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ubayd related to us, saying: Wasil al-Raqqashi related to us, from Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, regarding His words ﴿So do not say to them "uff," nor rebuke them﴾, he said: "Do not shake your hand at your parents." It is said of it: "nahara-hu yanharuhu nahran," and "intaharahu yantahiruhu intiharan."

As for His words ﴿and speak to them a generous word﴾, He, exalted is His praise, says: speak to them a fine, good word.

As:

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding ﴿and speak to them a generous word﴾: "The best word you can find."

al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman related to us, from Abdullah ibn al-Mukhtar, from Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, from Umar ibn al-Khattab, regarding ﴿a generous word﴾: "Do not refuse them anything they desire."

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This report is erroneous, I mean the report of Hisham ibn Urwa; it is from Hisham ibn Urwa, from his father, and there is no Umar in it. He related it from Ibn Ulayya and others, from Abdullah ibn al-Mukhtar.

Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, regarding ﴿and speak to them a generous word﴾: "That is, a soft, gentle word."

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, the same.

Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Harmala ibn Imran related to me, from Abu al-Haddaj al-Tujibi, who said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "Everything God the Mighty and Majestic mentioned in the Qur'an about dutifulness to parents, I know, except His words ﴿and speak to them a generous word﴾. What is this generous word?" Ibn al-Musayyab said: "The speech of a sinful slave to a harsh master."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verse 24:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾ (17:24)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Be humble toward them, out of mercy from you toward them, obeying them in what they command you, as long as it is not disobedience to God, and do not oppose them in what they love.

Those who held this view agreed with what we have said on this matter, the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil).

Mention of those who said that:

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, regarding His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾, he said: Do not refrain from anything they love.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Ash'ja'i narrated to us, saying: I heard Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, regarding His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾, he said: It is that you are gentle toward them, so that you do not refrain from anything they love.

Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam narrated to me, saying: Ayyub ibn Suwayd narrated to us, saying: al-Thawri narrated to us, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, regarding His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾, he said: Do not refrain from anything they love.

Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayyah narrated to us, from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mukhtar, from Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, regarding His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾, he said: It is that you do not refrain from anything they desire.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Muqri' Abu 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, from Harmalah ibn 'Imran, from Abu al-Hadadj, who said: I said to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾? He said: Have you not seen the words of the sinful slave to the harsh, coarse master? Al-Dhull (with a dammah on the dhal) and al-dhullah are both verbal nouns (masdar) from the word dhalil (humble, submissive). It means that one humbles oneself, and one is not humble by nature, from the speaker's saying: "I have humbled myself to you, I humble myself, a humbling and a humility," and this is like al-qull and al-qullah: when you drop the ha', you put a dammah on the dhal of al-dhull and on the qaf of al-qull, and when you keep the ha', you put a kasrah on the dhal of al-dhillah and on the qaf of al-qillah, as al-A'sha said:

"And I was not a qull before that, azyaban"

[[This is the second half of a verse by al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays (Diwan, Cairo edition, with commentary by Dr. Muhammad Husayn, p. 115), from a poem in which he satirises 'Amr ibn al-Mundhir ibn 'Abdan and reproaches the Banu Sa'd ibn Qays. Its first half is: "So they appeased him, if they gave him from me a grievance." In (Lisan al-'Arab: z-y-b) al-azyab means the claimant (al-da'i). Al-A'sha said, referring to a man of Qays 'Aylan who was a neighbour of 'Amr ibn al-Mundhir, and who had accused Hadaj, the al-A'sha's guide, of stealing his mount because he found some of its meat in his house; Hadaj was seized and beaten while al-A'sha was seated. Some people of that group stood up and took from al-A'sha the value of the mount, so al-A'sha said: "He called his kinsmen around me and they came to his aid, and I called my tribe, who were absent in the distance..."

"So they gave him from me half, or doubled it for him, and I was not a qull before that, azyaban."

That is, I was a stranger in that place, with no helper. Al-nisf means fairness. He says: they appeased him and gave him half or more. Al-qull among men means the base person, and from it is al-A'sha's saying. End of quotation.]]

He means al-qullah. As for al-dhill, with a kasrah on the dhal and the ha' dropped, it is a verbal noun from al-dhalul, from their saying: a dhalul animal, meaning clearly tame, that is, when it is gentle and not difficult.

From it is God's saying, may His praise be exalted: ﴿He it is who made the earth subservient to you﴾ (67:15), its plural being dhulul, as He said: ﴿Then follow the ways of your Lord, made easy﴾ (16:69). Mujahid interpreted this to mean that no place becomes rough for her when she travels it.

The reciters differed in reading this. The majority of reciters of the Hijaz, Iraq and Syria recited ﴿wa-ikhfid lahuma janah al-dhull﴾ with a dammah on the dhal, as a verbal noun from dhalil. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited ﴿janaha al-dhill﴾ with a kasrah on the dhal.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Bahz ibn Asad narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Awanah narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he recited ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ and said: Be humble to them, and do not be a tame animal to them.

Nasr ibn 'Ali narrated to us, saying: 'Umar ibn Shaqiq informed me, saying: I heard 'Asim al-Jahdari recite ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ and say: Be humble to them, and do not be a dhalul to them.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Umar ibn Shaqiq narrated to us, from 'Asim, the same.

Abu Ja'far said: According to this interpretation that 'Asim gave, his reading should have been with a dammah on the dhal, not with a kasrah; yet he read it with a kasrah.

Nasr and Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, and I was told from al-Farra', who said: Hushaym narrated to me, from Abu Bishr Ja'far ibn Iyas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, that he recited ﴿janaha al-dhill﴾. Al-Farra' said: al-Hakam ibn Zuhayr informed me, from 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, that he also recited it al-dhill. I asked Abu Bakr, and he said: 'Asim recited al-dhill.

As for His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾, He means: Supplicate God for your parents with mercy, and say: My Lord, have mercy on them, and show compassion toward them with Your forgiveness and Your mercy, just as they showed compassion toward me in my childhood, when they had mercy on me and brought me up as a child, until I became independent by myself and no longer needed them.

As follows:

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy and say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾, he said: Thus were you taught, and with this you were commanded. Take God's instruction and His discipline. It has been mentioned to us that "the Prophet of God (ﷺ) went out one day, extending his hands and raising his voice, saying: Whoever reaches his parents or one of them, and then enters the Fire afterward, may God distance him and destroy him." But they used to regard this as being dutiful to one's parents, and that in it was a little piety, for that leads to a great good. A group of the people of knowledge said: God's saying, the Exalted, ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾ is abrogated by His saying ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be close relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ (9:113).

Mention of those who said that:

'Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾ Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, sent down after this ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be close relatives﴾.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, from Yazid, from 'Ikrimah, who said concerning Surat Bani Isra'il ﴿Whether one or both of them reach old age with you﴾ ... up to His saying ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small."﴾ It was abrogated by the verse in Bara'ah ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be close relatives﴾ ... the verse.

al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said, regarding ﴿And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them"﴾ ... the verse, he said: It was abrogated by the verse in Bara'ah ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ ... the verse.

This verse may bear the meaning, although its apparent sense is general concerning all parents, without the meaning of abrogation, that its interpretation is particular, so that the meaning of the speech is: And say, "My Lord, have mercy upon them," if they are believers, as they brought me up when I was small. It is thus intended as particular, as we have said, and nothing of it has been abrogated. By His saying "brought me up" (rabbayani) He means "nurtured me" (nammayani).

The commentary on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him)﴾ [17:25]

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿Your Lord﴾, O people, ﴿knows best﴾ of you ﴿what is in your souls﴾ of veneration for your fathers and mothers and honouring them, and dutifulness toward them, and what is within them of believing that their rights may be treated lightly, and of disobedience toward them, and other inner thoughts of your breasts. Nothing of that is hidden from Him, and He will recompense you for its good and its evil. So beware of harbouring any ill toward them, or resolving upon disobedience to them.

* *

And His saying ﴿If you are righteous﴾:

He says: if you set your intentions right regarding them, and obey God in what He has commanded you concerning dutifulness toward them and fulfilling their rights upon you, after a lapse that came from you, or a slip in a duty owed to them, while maintaining what He has obligated upon you in His other obligations, then He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back after the slip and who repent after the lapse.

The people of interpretation (ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said regarding the interpretation of this.

Mention of those who said that:

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: I heard my father and my paternal uncle, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾, that he said: "It is a hasty word that a man may utter to his parents, not intending by it anything but good, so He said ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾."

Abu al-Sa'ib narrated to us, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, saying: My father informed me, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, with the like of it.

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: al-Hakam ibn Bashir narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, regarding His saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "It is the man from whom a hasty word comes toward his parents, while in his intention and heart he is not held accountable for it."

The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of His saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾.

Some of them said: They are those who glorify (God) (al-musabbihun).

Mention of those who said that:

Sulayman ibn Abd al-Jabbar narrated to me, saying: Muhammad ibn al-Salt narrated to us, saying: Abu Kudayna narrated to us; and Ibn Sinan al-Qazzaz narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn ibn al-Hasan al-Ashqar narrated to us, saying: Abu Kudayna narrated to us, from Ata, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "Those who glorify (God)."

al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abu Khaythama Zuhayr narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from Abu Maysara, from Amr ibn Shurahbil, who said: "The awwab is the one who glorifies (God)."

Others said: They are the obedient and the doers of good.

Mention of those who said that:

Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, his saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾: "He means: to the obedient doers of good."

Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "They are the obedient, and the people of prayer."

Ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "To the obedient who pray."

Others said: Rather, they are those who pray between sunset (maghrib) and the night prayer (isha').

Mention of those who said that:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, from Abu Sakhr Humayd ibn Ziyad, from Ibn al-Munkadir, traced back (to the Prophet), regarding ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "The prayer between sunset and the night prayer."

Others said: They are those who perform the forenoon prayer (duha).

Mention of those who said that:

Amr ibn Ali narrated to us, saying: Rabah Abu Sulayman al-Raqqa narrated to us, saying: I heard Awn al-Uqayli say regarding this verse ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾: "Those who perform the prayer of the forenoon."

Others said: Rather, it is the one who returns from his sin and repents from it.

Mention of those who said that:

Ahmad ibn al-Walid al-Qurashi narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, that he said regarding this verse ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾: "The one who commits a sin, then repents, then commits a sin, then repents."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Sulayman ibn Dawud narrated to us, from Shu'ba, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "He is the one who sins, then repents, then sins, then repents, in this verse ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾."

Mujahid ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id informed us, that he heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab being asked about this verse ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, and he said: "He is the one who sins, then repents, then sins, then repents."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Jarir ibn Hazim narrated to me, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, with its like.

Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, with its like.

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Malik narrated to me, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, regarding ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "He is the servant who sins, then repents, then sins, then repents."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: al-Layth ibn Sa'd informed me, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, who said: "I heard Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab say," and he mentioned the like of it.

al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri and Ma'mar informed us, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "The awwab is the one who sins, then repents, then sins, then repents, then sins, then repents."

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding this verse ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "Those who return to good."

Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Samad, Abu Dawud and Hisham narrated to us, from Shu'ba, from Abu Bishr, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, with its like.

Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us; and Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Amr, both from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, regarding ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "The one who recalls his sins in private, then seeks God's forgiveness for them."

al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, who said: "The awwab is the one who recalls his sins in private, then seeks God's forgiveness for them."

Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, that he said regarding this verse ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾: "The one who recalls his sin, then repents."

Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, both saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa' narrated to us, all from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying, may His praise be exalted, ﴿forgiving to those who turn back﴾: "The awwabun are those who return and repent."

al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Ibn Jurayj said, from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab: "The man who sins, then repents, three times."

Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Jarir narrated to us, from Mansur, from Mujahid, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, regarding His saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "The one who remembers his sins, then seeks God's forgiveness for them."

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Shurayh informed me, from Uqba ibn Muslim, from Ata ibn Yasar, that he said regarding His saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾: "The servant sins, then repents, and God accepts his repentance; then he sins, then repents, and God accepts his repentance; then he sins a third time, and if he repents, God accepts his repentance with a repentance that is not erased."

It has been related from Ubayd ibn Umayr a saying other than the one we mentioned from Mujahid, namely:

al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Muslim informed us, from Amr ibn Dinar, from Ubayd ibn Umayr, regarding His saying ﴿for indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back﴾, that he said: "We used to count the awwab as the one who guards himself, who says: O God, forgive me for what I committed in this gathering of mine."

The most correct of these sayings in interpretation is the saying of the one who said: The awwab is the one who repents from sin, who returns from disobedience of God to obedience to Him, and from what He hates to what He is pleased with. This is because the awwab is an intensive form (fa''al), from the speaker's saying: "So-and-so returned (aba) from such-and-such," either from his journey to his home, or from one state to another, as 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras said:

"Every absent one is expected to return, / but the one absent through death does not return."[[The verse is by 'Ubayd ibn al-Abras, the pre-Islamic poet (his Diwan, p. 7, Leiden edition, 1913), from his qasida whose opening is: "Empty of its people is Malhub." He means: every absent one is awaited to return, except the one who has died, for he has no return to this world. The verse is evidence that the awwab is one who returns, who turns back to repentance and obedience, from aba, ya'ubu, meaning to return (see Lisan al-Arab: awb). In the same place: Abu Bakr said regarding their saying "a man who is awwab," there are seven sayings: the merciful, the penitent, the one who glorifies (God), the one who returns to repentance and then sins and then repents, the obedient, and the one who recalls his sin in private and seeks God's forgiveness for it. End quote. All these meanings go back to the linguistic meaning, which is returning from one thing to another.]]

So he returns (ya'ubu) a return (awban), and he is a man who has returned (a'ib) from his journey, and an awwab from his sins.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 17, verses 26–27:

The interpretation of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And give the near of kin his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer, and do not squander wastefully. Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and the Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾

The exegetes differed concerning who is meant by His words ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾. Some of them said: it means the relatives of the deceased on both his father's and his mother's side. Allah, may His praise be exalted, commanded His servants to maintain ties with them.

Mention of those who said that:

● Imran ibn Musa narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id narrated to us, saying: Habib al-Mu'allim narrated to us, saying: A man asked al-Hasan, saying: "Shall I give my relatives the zakat of my wealth?" He said: "Indeed they have a right in that beyond the zakat." Then he recited this verse: ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾.

● Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ikrimah, regarding His words ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾, he said: "Its maintenance is what you intend to maintain them with, what you wish to do for them."

● Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿And give the near of kin his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾, he said: "It is that you maintain the kinsman and the needy, and show kindness to the wayfarer."

Others said: rather, it means the relatives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

Mention of those who said that:

● Muhammad ibn Umarah al-Asadi narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Aban narrated to us, saying: al-Sabbah ibn Yahya al-Muzani narrated to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu al-Dailam, who said: Ali ibn al-Husayn, peace be upon them both, said to a man from the people of Syria: "Have you recited the Qur'an?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Have you not read in (the chapter of) the Children of Israel: ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾?" He said: "And you are indeed the kinsfolk whose right Allah, may His praise be exalted, commanded to be given." He said: "Yes."

The more correct of the two interpretations in my view is the interpretation of those who understood it to mean the command of Allah to His servants to maintain the ties of their own relatives and kin on their fathers' and mothers' sides. This is because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, placed this immediately after His exhortation to His servants to be good to their fathers and mothers. Therefore it must be that this is an exhortation to maintain the ties of their own lineage, not the lineage of others which has not been mentioned. If that is so, the meaning of the speech is: "And give, O Muhammad, your near of kin his right of maintaining him, your kindness to him, and your goodness towards him." This was phrased as an address to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ, while what is intended by its ruling is everyone upon whom Allah's obligations are binding. This is shown by the opening of the injunction with His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and that you be good to parents. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you﴾. He directed the address with His words ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ to the Prophet of Allah ﷺ, then He said ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾, returning the address to all, then He turned the address with His words ﴿Whether one or both of them reach old age with you﴾ to addressing him alone. What is meant by all of that is everyone upon whom the obligations of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, are binding, whether the address is singular to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ alone, or general to him and all his community.

And His words ﴿and the needy﴾

This refers to the one who is humbled by need. We have already explained the meaning of the needy earlier, in a manner sufficient to avoid repeating it in this place.

And His words ﴿and the wayfarer﴾

That is: the traveller who has been cut off from his means. He, the Exalted, says: Maintain your kinsman and give him his right of maintenance; and the needy one in need, and the passer-by who has been cut off, help him and strengthen him to complete his journey. It has been said that the command to give the wayfarer his right is only that he be hosted for three days.

The first statement is in my view more correct, because Allah, the Exalted, did not specify any one of His rights over another in His Book, nor on the tongue of His Messenger; so it is general to every right which he is entitled to be given, whether hospitality, provision for riding, or assistance on his journey.

And His words ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾

He says: Do not, O Muhammad, scatter what Allah has given you of wealth in disobedience to Him, scattering it wastefully. The original meaning of tabdhir (squandering) is dispersal in extravagance; and from it is the saying of the poet:

"People who gave us protection, and their protection was like whirlwinds from the disobedience of the wasteful Iraq."
[[This is Mu'awiya ibn Sabra al-Sawa'i, Abu al-Ubaydin, diminutive of Ubaydan, the blind one of Kufa. He died in the year 98 AH. (From Khulasat al-Khazraji).]]

And according to what we have said regarding this, the exegetes have spoken.

Mention of those who said that:

● Muhammad ibn Ubayd al-Muharibi narrated to me, saying: Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu al-Ubaydin, who said: Abdullah said regarding His words ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾: "Squandering is in what is not right, and it is extravagance."

● Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Salamah, from Muslim al-Batin, from Abu al-Ubaydin, who said: Abdullah was asked about the squanderer, and he said: "Spending in what is not right."

● Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, from al-Hakam, who said: I heard Yahya ibn al-Jazzar narrating from Abu al-Ubaydin [[I have not identified the one who said this. It is said: "Fulan protected Fulan" when he defended him and prevented an oppressor from wronging him. Their jiwar (protection) here means their protection. Al-a'asir is the plural of i'sar, the wind that turns and carries dust and other things from the earth. Al-fisq: departure from obedience or from good conduct.

Al-mubaddhar: the passive participle of tabdhir, which is scattering wealth and the like and corrupting it through extravagance. In (Lisan al-Arab, root b-dh-r) it says: tabdhir is the corruption of wealth and its spending in extravagance. It has also been said: tabdhir is that wealth be spent on sins. End. On this meaning the author cited the verse.]], the blind one, that he asked Abdullah ibn Mas'ud about this verse ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾, and he said: "Spending wealth in what is not its right."

● Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Abi Za'idah narrated to me, saying: Ibn Idris narrated to us, from al-A'mash, from al-Hakam, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, from Abu al-Ubaydin, from Abdullah, the like of it.

● Ya'qub narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ulayyah narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah informed us, from al-Hakam ibn Utaybah, from Yahya ibn al-Jazzar, that Abu al-Ubaydin was blind, and he asked Ibn Mas'ud, saying: "What is tabdhir?" He said: "Spending wealth in what is not its right."

● Khallad ibn Aslam narrated to us, saying: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl informed us, saying: al-Mas'udi informed us, saying: Salamah ibn Kuhayl informed us, from Abu al-Ubaydin, and he had an affliction, and Abdullah knew of that about him, and he said: "O Abu Abd al-Rahman, what is tabdhir?" and he mentioned the like of it.

● Ahmad ibn Mansur al-Ramadi narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Haw'ab narrated to us, from Ammar ibn Zuraiq, from Abu Ishaq, from Harithah ibn Mudrib, from Abu al-Ubaydin, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "We, the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, used to say that tabdhir is spending in what is not its right."

● Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Kathir al-Anbari narrated to us, saying: Shu'bah narrated to us, saying: I was walking with Abu Ishaq on the road to Kufa, when he came upon a house being built with plaster and bricks, and he said: "This is tabdhir according to the saying of Abdullah: spending wealth in what is not its right."

● Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾, he said: "The squanderer is one who spends in what is not its right."

● Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abbad narrated to us, from Husayn, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "The squanderer is one who spends in what is not its right."

● Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Ata al-Khurasani, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Do not spend in falsehood, for the squanderer is one who is extravagant in what is not right."

Ibn Juraij said: Mujahid said: "If a person spent all his wealth in what is right, it would not be tabdhir; and if he spent a mudd in falsehood, it would be tabdhir."

● Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words ﴿and do not squander wastefully﴾, he said: "Tabdhir is spending in disobedience to Allah, in what is not right, and in corruption."

● Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿And give the near of kin his right, and the needy, and the wayfarer﴾: "He began with the parents before this; when he finished with the parents and their right, he mentioned these, and said ﴿do not squander wastefully﴾: do not give in the disobedience of Allah."

As for His words ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾, it means: indeed, those who scatter their wealth in disobedience to Allah, spending it in what is not His obedience, are the allies of the devils. Likewise the Arabs say of everyone who keeps to the way of a people and follows their trail: "He is their brother." ﴿And the Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: he says, the Satan was ungrateful for the blessing of his Lord which He bestowed upon him, denying it and not thanking Him for it; rather he rejects it by abandoning obedience to Allah and committing His disobedience. Likewise his brothers among the children of Adam who squander their wealth in the disobedience of Allah do not thank Allah for His blessings upon them, but oppose His command and disobey Him, and follow the example of the Satan in what Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has bestowed upon them of wealth which He entrusted to them, by abandoning gratitude for it and meeting it with ingratitude.

Like the one who:

● Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, who said: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿Indeed, the squanderers﴾: those who spend in the disobedience of Allah ﴿are brothers of the devils, and the Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾.
